title: the line
hook: a line that isn't in the oldest text has become a word millions of people use every day
carry: some lines are there to protect

segments.voice: Yesterday: the line, part one. In Valmiki there's no line: Lakshmana, wounded by Sita's frightened words, left her in the care of the forest spirits: let the forest be my witness, he said. Did you answer someone's fear instead of their words? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Open an Indian newspaper and you may find it in a headline. A court warns the government not to cross the Lakshman rekha. A columnist says some joke crossed the Lakshman rekha. A parent tells a teenager: that's the Lakshman rekha, curfew is eleven. Lakshmana's line, a limit you must not cross. It's become part of everyday speech. And yesterday we saw that in Valmiki's Ramayana, the line doesn't exist. So where did it come from?
screen: `A WORD IN THE HEADLINES.` → `A LIMIT YOU MUST NOT CROSS.` → `SO WHERE DID IT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana was never only one book. It was retold in Tamil, Bengali, Telugu, Hindi and other languages, in songs, plays, temple carvings, and village performances. Each telling kept the bones of the story and added its own flesh. The line belongs to that later life of the story. One well-known witness is Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the retelling in Awadhi, an older form of Hindi. And here's a curious thing. Even in Tulsidas, the line isn't drawn on stage, in the forest scene itself. It's mentioned later, by Ravana's wife, Mandodari, as she pleads with him before the war. You couldn't even cross the little line Rama's younger brother drew, she says. How will you face Rama? From hints like that, and from storytellers and folk tradition, the scene grew. Ramlila performers acted it out. Painters painted it. And television serials put it in front of huge audiences: Lakshmana drawing a glowing line with his arrow. None of this makes one telling right and the other wrong. Hindus have long lived with many Ramayanas side by side. Valmiki gives Lakshmana's trust in the forest spirits. The later tellings give a line in the dust. Both are trying to say the same thing: some boundaries are there to protect you, and the danger comes when they're crossed.
screen: `NEVER ONLY ONE BOOK.` · `TULSIDAS: MANDODARI'S WORDS.` · `RAMLILA, PAINTINGS, TELEVISION.` · `MANY RAMAYANAS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `SOME LINES ARE THERE TO PROTECT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Picture a line drawn around you on the floor, a circle just wide enough for your body. Inside it, for these two minutes, nothing is asked of you. Breathe there. Then think of one boundary in your own life that protects you or someone else: a bedtime, a no you've learned to say, a time you put the phone away. Don't judge whether you keep it well. Just honor that it's there. The bell holds the time.
The line. Lakshman rekha: absent from Valmiki, mentioned by Mandodari in Tulsidas, and now an everyday word for a limit not to be crossed.
Your line: some lines are there to protect. Today, keep one boundary that protects you, and respect one that protects someone else. Day five hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: The Lakshman rekha is a common phrase in Hindi and Indian English for a limit not to be crossed, and the drawn line is a familiar scene in Ramlila performances and popular retellings.

original.note: Hindi lakṣmaṇ rekhā: Lakshmana's line. rekhā means a line or a drawn mark.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Lakshman rekha is in every Ramayana.
what it means: it's absent from Valmiki and grew in later tellings.
what a scholar hears: in the Ramcharitmanas, the line appears in Mandodari's words in the Lanka Kanda, not as an on-stage scene in the forest.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 45 (no line; Lakshmana entrusts Sita to the forest deities)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kanda (Mandodari: the little line drawn by Rama's younger brother)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kanda (Lakshmana entrusts Sita to the forest and its deities)

notes: Confirm the Ramcharitmanas reference: Mandodari's line about the 'laghu rekha' drawn by Rama's younger brother (Lanka Kanda, around doha 35–36), and that the Manas's Aranya Kanda scene itself has no drawn line.
'One well-known early witness' is deliberately cautious: whether earlier regional tellings (e.g. in Bengali, Telugu or folk traditions) have the line should be checked.
Television serials of the 1980s (e.g. Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan) are referred to without naming; confirm the scene appears there.
Example headlines are illustrative of usage, not quotations.

Reviewer: myth answer softened from 'folk tellings carried it long before television' to what is documented (Tulsidas; Ramlila). How old the drawn-line scene is in folk and regional tellings needs a Keeper's check.
